source.title: Compute Optimal Tokenization
source.authors: Tomasz Limisiewicz; Artidoro Pagnoni; Srinivasan Iyer; Mike Lewis; Sachin Mehta; Alisa Liu; Margaret Li; Gargi Ghosh; Luke S. Zettlemoyer

record.file_problem: No apparent garbling or cutoff; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study directly measures held-out language-model loss across compute, data, parameter, and compression settings, using a new experimental design to examine scaling and compute-optimal allocation.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the paper's own loss fits, allocation fits, extrapolation evaluation, language comparisons, and stated downstream-task comparisons. Related-work results cited from other papers are not recorded as findings. Architecture recipes are described but not compared as a test of architecture-shape sensitivity.
record.test_reason: The study runs its own IsoFLOP sweeps (988 BLT and 320 subword models, 5e18–2e21 FLOPs) on held-out C4 BPB. It fits compute-optimal data/parameter power laws and an optimal-loss power law in compute, and checks extrapolation to a held-out 2e21 budget. These are its own results on V1, V2, V3 and V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that compute-optimal English training holds about 60 training bytes per parameter, constant across compute and compression. This generalises the Chinchilla proportional rule, whose 20 tokens per parameter holds only for BPE-like compression. An optimal compression rate exists, is domain-specific and decreases slowly with compute. These trends hold for latent and subword tokenization. Optimal ratios also vary by language with parity.
record.recipe_differences: The paper runs its own scaling sweep using BLT latent tokenization and several subword tokenizers; it does not reproduce Kaplan et al. or Hoffmann et al.'s original experimental recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: The measured optimum changes with compression rate, tokenizer family, language, compute budget, and monolingual versus joint multilingual training. The fitted extrapolation quality also changes with the chosen residual form.

fits_no_version.finding: At each compute budget there is a loss-minimising compression rate. For BLT it is about 3.7 at 1e20 and 3.3 at 2e21 FLOPs, and it decreases slowly with compute. Masked-vocabulary BPE beats original BPE at high compute.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The compute-optimal tokenizer compression rate exists and decreases slowly with training compute.

fits_no_version.finding: At matched inference cost, a 3.3B model at T=4 scores 74.1% on HellaSwag vs 68.2% for a 6.7B model at T=8. ARC-Easy and ARC-Challenge show task-dependent compression preferences.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The downstream benefit of tokenizer compression depends on task and inference-cost matching.

record.problems: The main power-law fits are empirical fits over the tested ranges; the claimed extrapolation is evaluated only at 2 × 10^21 FLOPs after fitting up to 1 × 10^21 FLOPs. The paper fixes most training hyperparameters rather than tuning them by budget. Some downstream results are presented in figures without numerical values. Language-specific results use a fixed 10^20 FLOPs budget.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows omitted. Downstream benchmark plots without a textual numeric comparison are not given separate rows unless the text states the comparison.

untested.parts: Separate power laws in parameters or tokens with the others non-bottlenecked. Only optimal loss vs compute (about 2.6 orders of magnitude) is fit.
Extrapolation over orders of magnitude. The held-out budget is only 2x the largest fitted budget.
Token-based allocation as in Kaplan and Hoffmann. The allocation law is fit in bytes and latent-module parameters; the Kaplan parameter-faster-than-data split is not reproduced.
Entire version. The width/depth recipe is fixed; local-module shape choices are not compared at fixed parameter count.
Entire version. Downstream tasks are reported only at one budget, against inference cost.
Training schedule, learning-rate tuning and fitting-method variation (hyperparameters are fixed across runs).

missing.what: Optimal ρ⋆ is about 60 across tokenization methods: latent entropy 62.1, latent fixed-size 60.0, subword 58.8. The subword T⋆ is skewed by the character-model fit.
Authors note constant ρ⋆ is more visible for C>1e20, where global-module compute dominates. Allocation is less stable at small budgets.
Observed lowest BPB per compute budget and compression (latent), not derived from the law.
Parameter-counting convention differs between fits: Law I uses latent-module parameters only, Law II uses total compute.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. The results align with Hoffmann's equal scaling (in bytes), not Kaplan's split. Hyperparameters are fixed (no learning-rate tuning per budget). Extrapolation was tested only at 2x compute.

versions.untested_parts: The study fits optimal loss against compute and evaluates loss over data/parameter IsoFLOP configurations; it does not separately establish a loss power law in parameters or tokens while the other quantities are non-bottlenecks.
The held-out compute budget is 2 × 10^21 FLOPs after fitting to budgets up to 1 × 10^21 FLOPs, so this does not test extrapolation by orders of magnitude.

The main allocation law is expressed in bytes and latent-module parameters; it does not test Kaplan et al.'s parameter-faster-than-data trend, nor a token-based allocation law across different compression rates.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
The paper studies text pretraining; it does not test other modalities, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer scaling laws.
Downstream benchmarks are evaluated, but the paper does not test whether downstream performance is predictably related to scale or pretraining loss.

The paper compares tokenization methods, languages, and residual-fit forms, but does not systematically vary parameter-counting conventions, training schedules, or all other fitting choices, nor test whether published laws disagree across a common replicated setup.

rows.size_stated: 50M to 6.7B parameters across the experiments
rows.operation_detail: Fit compute-optimal data amount as a power law of compute and compression, then derive optimal parameter count.
rows.measure: Fitted optimal data and parameter scaling exponents
rows.value: B0 = 17.5, N0 = 9.5 × 10−3, α = 0.465, β = 0.471; N⋆ is derived with compute exponent 1−α and compression exponent 1−β.
rows.uncertainty: not stated for these latent-fit parameters
rows.note: The fitted exponents for data in bytes and parameters are close to 0.5, consistent with approximately proportional growth in bytes and parameters.
rows.check: Fine. α=0.465 (near 0.5) supports equal scaling in bytes. β=0.471 (not 1) shows the token-based split depends on compression.

rows.size_stated: 50M to 6.7B parameters across the experiments
rows.operation_detail: Fit loss laws on lower-compute runs and evaluate predicted loss on a higher-compute budget.

conditions.value: 48 runs with budgets up to 1 × 10^21 FLOPs

rows.measure: Extrapolation RMSE and fit statistics for alternative residual forms
rows.baseline: Mean residual model: RMSE = 0.0260, R² = 0.903, adjusted R² = 0.896
rows.value: Constant optimal compression: RMSE = 0.0115, R² = 0.996, adjusted R² = 0.995. Compute-dependent optimal compression: RMSE = 0.0086, R² = 0.997, adjusted R² = 0.996.
rows.note: The compute-dependent residual form predicts the held-out budget better than the two alternatives, but the held-out budget is only twice the largest fit budget, not orders of magnitude larger.
rows.check: For the compute-dependent form, extrapolation error is low (RMSE 0.0086), so 'observed' fits the 2x range tested. 'Partial' conflated the untested orders-of-magnitude range with the result. The mean-residual (classical irreducible-loss) form extrapolates about 3x worse.
